title: The use of ChatGPT as a learning tool to improve foreign language writing in a multilingual and multicultural classroom
venue: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether ChatGPT can function as a feedback tool to improve second/foreign language writing, especially for socially vulnerable learners with refugee or migrant backgrounds. The research question focuses on the extent to which ChatGPT can help improve L2 writing in vocabulary and grammar for these students.

The intervention involved a short classroom writing cycle using ChatGPT for feedback. Students first wrote a personal email in German about their favourite sport. Researchers then used ChatGPT to improve the students’ texts specifically in vocabulary and grammar. Students reviewed the revised versions, discussed the changes and suggestions, and then wrote a second email on a similar topic about sports and healthy life. The study compared the first and second writing products using quantitative text features: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words.

The study was conducted over two weeks in a single junior high school in Patras, Greece. Participants were eight 15-year-old students with refugee/migrant backgrounds enrolled in German as a foreign language. They were attending the third grade of Junior High School, had studied German for five years, and were at approximately A2 level. The school served a multilingual and multicultural student population, including students with refugee/migrant backgrounds.

The authors conclude that ChatGPT showed promise as a language-learning and feedback tool for L2 writing. After the intervention, students’ second texts generally contained more total words, more unique words, and longer sentences, which the authors interpret as improvement in writing performance, vocabulary use, and grammar-related output. At the same time, they emphasize that this was a pilot study with a very small sample and short duration, so the findings should be treated cautiously and verified through larger studies in more diverse contexts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small pilot classroom study with n=8, no control group, short duration, and outcomes based on descriptive before/after writing metrics rather than validated external assessments. It provides direct K-12 evidence, but credibility is limited by design and measurement concerns.
impact_tier_rationale: The study reports promising but unclear impact: improvements were observed in writing-process/product metrics for a priority population (migrant/refugee secondary students in EFL learning), yet no standardized effect size, external literacy gain, or durable post-removal evidence was established.

interventions.use_case: ChatGPT was used as an AI feedback and revision tool to improve German-as-a-foreign-language student emails by enhancing vocabulary and grammar, after which students rewrote on a similar topic.

ChatGPT functioned as a generative AI conversational system that produced revised versions of students' texts and linguistic suggestions, but the study centered more specifically on writing feedback than on dialogic tutoring.

finding.finding_summary: In a pilot study with 8 junior high school students (age 15) with migrant/refugee backgrounds learning German as a foreign language, post-support writing samples on a similar topic were longer and lexically richer than initial drafts after students reviewed ChatGPT-improved versions of their texts. Mean total word count increased by 38%, unique words increased by an average of 19.1 words per student, and average words per sentence increased by about 42%; however, no standardized literacy assessment, rubric-scored writing quality measure, or inferential effect size was reported.
finding.measure: Process/product text metrics from student writing samples: total words, unique words, average words per sentence, and most frequent words
